text: Shifting security left means asking what could go wrong before a single line of code exists. Threat modeling is the structured way to ask that question. This lesson walks through the core idea using Northbridge Retail's new checkout service as the running example — a system that accepts customer payment details, which makes it exactly the kind of system you'd want to threat model before building.

A threat model is a structured answer to four questions, usually in this order. What are we building — a diagram of the system. What can go wrong — a list of threats against that diagram. What are we going to do about it — mitigations, prioritized. And did we do a good enough job — a review, repeated as the system changes. The first question matters more than it sounds, because the diagram is what reveals where risk actually concentrates.

Draw Northbridge's checkout flow as boxes and arrows: a customer's browser, the checkout web service, a payment processing API, an order database, and an inventory service. Draw a dashed line anywhere the level of trust changes — between the public internet and Northbridge's network, between checkout and the payment processor. Those dashed lines are trust boundaries, and every arrow crossing one is a place an attacker would look first. This picture, made precise, is a data flow diagram.

STRIDE gives you six categories of threat to check against each boundary crossing: Spoofing, pretending to be a legitimate user or service; Tampering, modifying data in transit or at rest; Repudiation, denying an action with no audit trail to counter it; Information disclosure, seeing data you shouldn't; Denial of service, making the system unavailable; and Elevation of privilege, gaining capabilities you shouldn't have. A finding against the public checkout API outranks the same finding against a rarely-used internal dashboard — threat modeling makes that tradeoff deliberate, not accidental, and it's cheapest to fix while it's still a whiteboard decision instead of a deployed service.
Next up, Chapter 2: least-privilege identity, starting with the IAM principles that decide who, and what service, gets to touch Northbridge's checkout flow in the first place.
